extracted.intended_audience: federal agencies, OPM and agency HR officials, federal legal counsel, and members of the public commenting on OPM rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal analysis regarding OPM's proposed regulations on moving positions and employees between the competitive and excepted civil service, including limits of authority, statutory interactions, employee rights, and procedural requirements. Useful for agencies implementing the rule, affected employees, and commenters evaluating legality and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of OPM regulatory authority (Title 5 only)
rubrics_metrics.description: OPM's authorities to issue regulations only extend to title 5, U.S. Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proposed regulations apply to any situation where an agency moves positions or people from the competitive service to the excepted service, or between excepted services, whether pursuant to statute, Executive order, or an OPM issuance, to the extent that these provisions are not inconsistent with applicable statutory provisions. For example, to the extent that a position is placed in the excepted service by an act of Congress, an OPM regulation will not supersede a statutory provision to the contrary. However, an OPM regulation may prescribe the procedures by which agencies would be required to move positions unless inconsistent with that statutory provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability when positions shift between titles
rubrics_metrics.description: These regulatory provisions also apply where positions previously governed by title 5 will be governed by another title going forward, unless the statute governing the exception provides otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regs follow the position unless a statutory provision governing the exception says otherwise; OPM's regulatory reach is limited by the underlying statute for the position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between probationary period and trial period
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'probationary period' generally applies to employees in the competitive service. 'Trial period' applies to employees in the excepted service and some appointments in the competitive service (such as term appointments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fundamental difference between the two is the duration in which employees must serve. The probationary period is set by law to last 1 year. When the trial period is set by individual agencies, it can last up to 2 years. See 5 CFR 315.801 through 806; see also MSPB, Navigating the Probationary Period After Van Wersch and McCormick (Sept. 2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political appointee status and exclusion from civil service protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Political appointees serve at the pleasure of the President or other appointing official and may be asked to resign or be dismissed at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are not covered by civil service removal procedures, have no adverse action rights, and generally have no right to appeal terminations. See e.g., 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) and 5 CFR provisions excluding noncareer, political appointees from adverse action protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment rights in reduction-in-force (competitive vs. excepted service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees in the competitive service have assignment rights (bumping/retreating) in a reduction in force; excepted service employees have no assignment rights unless the agency chooses to offer them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive-service employees reached for release during an RIF are entitled to offers of assignment if they have bump or retreat rights to an available position in the same competitive area. 'Bumping' means displacement of an employee in a lower tenure group or subgroup; 'retreating' means displacement in the same tenure group and subgroup. See 5 CFR 351.501 and .502. Despite differences, merit system principles remain central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veterans' preference as congressional mandate for competitive hiring
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedures Congress adopted for hiring in the competitive service were designed, in part, to implement the stated congressional policy of veterans' preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 5 U.S.C. 1302 and related hiring statutes and regulations; how that mandate is realized should be considered when positions are moved into noncompetitive processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation requirement for hiring criteria and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Validation generally requires that the criteria and methods by which job applicants are evaluated have a rational relationship to performance in the position to be filled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 5 CFR part 300. Agencies must ensure selection procedures are job-related and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for excepting positions: 'conditions of good administration' / necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions from the competitive service are permissible when 'conditions of good administration' warrant; OPM may depart from the norm only when necessary for those conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have reinforced that filling positions through competitive process is the norm and departure requires necessity for 'conditions of good administration' (quoting 5 U.S.C. 3302). An agency's assertion (e.g., cost of developing exam) must be supported by evidence sufficient to meet the standard of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory vs. Executive/OPM authority and APA constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to regulate under chapter 75 is conferred directly upon OPM (e.g., 5 U.S.C. 7514) whereas section 3302 confers rulemaking on the President for the competitive service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A President could order the Director of OPM to promulgate regulations relating to chapter 75, but any such rule would then be subject to the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act. Compare 5 U.S.C. 7514 to 5 U.S.C. 3302 for differences in source of authority and procedural constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits when Congress has placed a position in the excepted service
rubrics_metrics.description: When a position is placed in the excepted service by an act of Congress, OPM regulation will not supersede a contrary statutory provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM may still prescribe procedures unless inconsistent with the statutory placement; legislative placement controls over regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSC investigative authority and MSPB corrective remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: OSC investigates allegations of prohibited personnel practices and may petition the MSPB for corrective action if an agency does not satisfactorily correct the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If OSC proves its claim, the MSPB may order the corrective action it deems appropriate. See 5 U.S.C. 1214(a)(1)(A), (a)(5) and 1214(b)(2)(B), (C), (b)(4)(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to challenge prohibited personnel practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to a personnel action on the basis that it constitutes a prohibited personnel practice may be brought by anyone in a covered position, regardless of their entitlement to adverse action rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 5 U.S.C. 2302(a)(1), (a)(2), (b). This means noncareer or excepted employees may still be able to contest certain improper personnel actions under the prohibited practices framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating' character
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrases describing positions that may be excepted (e.g., 'confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, policy-advocating') have historically been given a much narrower meaning than an expansive reading that would capture most career positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.O. language stating that incumbents are entrusted with non-public information cannot alone be the sole standard for 'confidential' because virtually all positions have non-public information obligations; courts and Congress have long read the phrases more narrowly. See discussion of E.O. 13957 and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process and property-right protections recognized by courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized due process rights and, in some cases, that restrictions on loss of employment can create a property right warranting constitutional protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites to cases such as Board of Regents v. Roth, Slochower, Wieman, Connell, and others demonstrate that public employees have challenged removals historically and that statutory employment protections may be enforceable under various legal theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routes for judicial review and appeals depending on claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate appellate forum varies: MSPB appeals, Federal Circuit, other circuit courts, or Federal district courts depending on the nature of the claim (e.g., whistleblower retaliation, discrimination statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See statutes such as 5 U.S.C. 7703 and discussion: the appropriate federal appellate court will generally be the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit but some claims may be appealed to other circuits or to district courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory best practices during probationary/trial periods
rubrics_metrics.description: OPM guidance recommends agencies remind supervisors/managers about the value of the probationary period and make an affirmative decision regarding the probationer's fitness for continued employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See OPM guidance on Maximizing Effective Use of Probationary Periods: periodically remind supervisors, make affirmative decisions, and follow good management practices during this critical assessment opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit system principles as foundational standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit system principles are at the core of civil service protections relating to hiring, conduct, and performance matters as applied to both career competitive and excepted service employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with statutory and procedural differences between competitive and excepted service protections, agencies should apply merit system principles when managing hiring, conduct, and performance.
